title: Two Equal Halves With Closest Sums
statement:
You get an array nums of 2n integers. Split it into two groups of exactly n numbers each; every number goes into exactly one group, and positions do not matter.

Return the smallest possible absolute difference between the sums of the two groups. Numbers can be negative.

examples.why: {3, 9} against {7, 3} gives 12 and 10. Putting the two 3s together gives 6 and 16.
With n = 1 there is only one split: |−8 − 5| = 13.
The total is 20, but no three numbers add up to exactly 10. {1, 4, 6} = 11 against {10, −3, 2} = 9 is as close as it gets.

hints: Trying every way to choose n of 2n numbers is up to C(30, 15) ≈ 155 million splits, too many. What if you split the array itself in half first?
Suppose the first group takes c numbers from the left half. Then it takes exactly n − c from the right half. For each half, list all subset sums grouped by how many numbers they use: only 2¹⁵ each.
For a left sum a with c numbers, you want a right sum b with n − c numbers that makes a + b as close as possible to total / 2. Sort each right list once and binary search.

explain.intuition:
The group sums are tied together: if one group sums to s, the other sums to total − s, so the difference is |total − 2s|. The job is to pick n numbers whose sum is as close as possible to half the total. With negatives allowed there is no useful pruning or small-sum DP, and choosing n of 2n directly is too many options.

Meet in the middle: cut the array into a left half and a right half of n numbers each. Any group takes some c numbers from the left and n − c from the right. Each half has only 2ⁿ subsets, about 32 000 for n = 15. Group the right half's subset sums by size and sort them. Then, for every left subset with sum a and size c, binary-search the right list of size n − c for the sum nearest to total / 2 − a.
steps: Split into L = nums[0..n) and R = nums[n..2n). Let total be the sum of all numbers.
For each half, compute the sum of every subset and store it in a list indexed by subset size. Sort the right lists.
For each left subset with size c and sum a: in right[n − c], binary search the first sum b with 2(a + b) ≥ total.
Check that b and the one just before it; update the best with |total − 2(a + b)|.
Return the best value. It can stop early at 0.
pitfalls: Using a subset-sum DP over values. With values up to 10⁷ and negatives the table is far too big.
Pairing a left subset with right subsets of any size. The group must have exactly n numbers, so sizes must add up to n.
Checking only the found index. The closest sum may be just below the target, so look at the neighbour before it too.

solutions.title: Try every group of n
solutions.idea: Enumerate every subset of 2n positions with exactly n members and measure |total − 2·sum|.

solutions.title: Meet in the middle with binary search
solutions.idea: Enumerate subset sums of each half by size. For each left subset of size c, binary search the sorted right sums of size n − c for the one that brings the group closest to half the total.

followups: Drop the equal-size rule: any split into two groups. What changes, and when does a sum DP become usable?
Return the actual groups, not only the difference.
